newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Accused New Zealand gunman a mental health patient.
newsitem.headline: Accused New Zealand gunman a mental health patient.

text.p: New Zealand health authorities said on Monday a man charged in the killing of one of six people slain in a weekend shotgun shooting massacre was a mental health patient.

Police arrested Stephen Anderson, stark naked in the tiny central North Island rural and resort settlement of Raurimu on Saturday and charged him with one count of murder after the shootings, in which six people were killed and five seriously wounded.
They said other charges were pending and no other suspects were being sought.

"Capital Coast Health can confirm that Stephen Anderson has been a patient of our Mental Health Service. Issues of natural justice mean further details cannot be released," said Dr John Gleisner, the leader of mental health for the Wellington region.
Family and friends said Anderson, 22, was diagnosed as schizophrenic last year, and the family was devastated by this news.

His father, Neville Anderson, was among those killed at the tiny resort and farming town of Raurimu in the central North Island. His mother, Helen Anderson, was reported to have been one of six out of a gathering of 18 friends and family who escaped unharmed.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger said the Raurimu shootings would be taken into account in a review of gun laws already under way as a result of the Port Arthur and Dunblane shootings in Australia and Britain.
The murders occurred in and near Raurimu Lodge, which was built by Neville Anderson and where the friends and family had come from Wellington for a weekend retreat in peaceful surroundings.
A woman family friend told Radio New Zealand the parents wanted to give their son the best life possible, including taking him on regular hiking holidays and ensuring he had a good education.
Neighbours painted a picture of a kind, friendly couple.
The Andersons live in one of the most exclusive streets of Khandallah, one of Wellington's most expensive suburbs, and resided in one of its most exclusive streets.
After problems adjusting at the local high school, they sent Stephen to the exclusive Rathkeale College.

The New Zealand health service, particularly the Mental Health Service, has meanwhile come under extreme scrutiny for opening up mental health institutions and looking after patients in the community rather than in hospitals and institutions.

Critics say the move was undertaken for economic reasons and that while sick people may improve faster within the community, the service did not provide adequate help, and in many cases no help at all.
Former prime minister and senior opposition MP Mike Moore said New Zealand's mental health programmes were in crisis.

"The care of acutely disturbed psychiatric patients outside hospitals in what is dishonestly called the community has not worked and has been discredited internationally as a failed experiment," he said.
Ian Garratt, a long-time friend of the Andersons, said Neville Anderson was having breakfast when the gunfire started.
"They were all having breakfast. The gunman came into the ski lodge through this one door in the back with a shotgun.
"The gunman just presented the shotgun at Nev (Neville Anderson) and Nev walked over to him and grabbed the front of the barrel and he pulled the trigger.
"From there on he didn't stop," he said.
Police Inspector Jeff Holloway said in Raurimu that police were still investigating and would probably remove the remaining bodies on Monday.
